How often does a repeated random permutation fail to mix?

Take one uniformly random permutation PP of the N=2nN=2^n points of V=𝔽2nV=\mathbb F_2^n and reuse it in every round, with fresh independent XOR keys. Let ft(n)f_t(n) be the probability that some starting ordered tuple of tt distinct points fails to converge to uniform on all such tuples. All probabilities in this note are over the choice of PP. The question concerns eventual convergence, rather than a prescribed number of rounds.

Result. Uniformly over 2≤t≤N−22\le t\le N-2, as n→∞n\to\infty,

ft(n)∼2(N−1)(NN/2)∼2πN3/22−N. f_t(n)\sim \frac{2(N-1)}{\binom N{N/2}} \sim \sqrt{2\pi}\,N^{3/2}2^{-N}.

Conditional on failure, the probability that PP preserves at least one parity partition tends to one. This explains the scale change visible from three bits to four. At five bits the probability of pairwise failure is between 1.0314758815164×10−71.0314758815164\times10^{-7} and 1.0314762567980×10−71.0314762567980\times10^{-7}, roughly one permutation in 9.69 million. These decimal endpoints have been rounded outwards. A separate exact five-bit count now determines the probability inside this interval. The finite interval is proved below independently of the asymptotic error estimate.

Prior art and scope

Babai and Hayes prove that adjoining one uniform permutation to a group with o(N)o(N) common fixed points generates ANA_N or SNS_N with probability tending to one. The translations act transitively. Their theorem, together with the orbit argument below, already gives ft(n)=o(1)f_t(n)=o(1) simultaneously for 2≤t≤N−22\le t\le N-2. Eberhard, Ford and Koukoulopoulos estimate a different event in which the transitive subgroup containing a random permutation can be chosen without fixing its translation group. The fixed translations are essential to the much smaller probability computed here. Babai–Hayes, Theorem 1 (2006) · Eberhard–Ford–Koukoulopoulos, Theorems 1.1 and 1.3 (2016)

The proof combines the published key-alternating coset obstruction with two published bounds on primitive permutation groups. Li gives a structural classification of primitive groups containing a regular abelian subgroup. Bounds on group orders and numbers of group actions suffice here, without cataloguing all those types or assuming that the given translations are the socle of an affine group. The quantitative equivalent, the quotient expansion, and the finite interval are project derivations. Independent publication priority remains unverified. Caranti–Dalla Volta–Sala, Corollary 3.3 · Li (2003) · Maróti, Corollary 1.1 · Pyber–Shalev (1997)

Why a fixed parity split dominates

Let TT be the group of binary translations, G=⟨T,P⟩G=\langle T,P\rangle, and HH the normal closure of TT in GG. The walk mixes on ordered tt-tuples exactly when HH is tt-transitive. Grouping rounds into blocks of length equal to the order of PP gives this criterion. The quotient G/HG/H is cyclic, generated by the image of PP. Consequently G′G' lies in HH. If GG contains ANA_N and N≥5N\ge5, the perfect group ANA_N lies in HH, and ANA_N is transitive on ordered distinct tt-tuples for t≤N−2t\le N-2. Two unused points allow either parity of a completion. Full group-and-walk proof

Conversely, if GG is imprimitive, its blocks are the cosets of a proper nonzero binary subspace WW. Translations force this form: translating the block of zero by one of its elements gives the same block. Preserving the partition leaves all nonzero differences in WW trapped there. Pairwise nonmixing implies nonmixing on tt-tuples by taking a marginal. We have sandwiched failure between imprimitivity and imprimitivity plus the event that GG is primitive and excludes ANA_N.

A nonzero linear functional hh defines a parity split into two halves. Its stabilizer allows independently permuting each half and exchanging the halves. Its probability is 2/(NN/2)2/\binom{N}{N/2}. There are N−1N-1 such splits. For two distinct masks, their joint map to two bits has four equal fibers. Keeping both splits fixes the two output bits up to a translation, giving probability 4((N/4)!)4/N!4((N/4)!)^4/N!. Thus the sum of the single probabilities approximates their union with absolute error at most

(N−12)4((N/4)!)4N!=exp(−Nlog4+O(logN)). \binom{N-1}{2}\,4\,\frac{((N/4)!)^4}{N!} =\exp(-N\log4+O(\log N)).

For a fixed subspace of codimension dd with q=2dq=2^d cosets of size b=N/qb=N/q, the full stabilizer has q!(b!)qq!(b!)^q elements. Here is a bound useful for every fixed integer k≥1k\ge1. The probability that some nonzero proper subspace of codimension d≥k+1d\ge k+1 has its cosets preserved is at most

exp(−(k+1)Nlog2+ok(N)). \exp\bigl(-(k+1)N\log 2+o_k(N)\bigr).

Indeed, for q≤Nq\le\sqrt N, factorial estimates give log(q!(b!)q/N!)=−Nlogq+O(qlogN)\log(q!(b!)^q/N!)=-N\log q+O(q\log N). For q>Nq>\sqrt N, use N!≥(N/e)NN!\ge(N/e)^N, b!≤bbb!\le b^b and q!≤qqq!\le q^q. The log probability is at most N−(N−q)logq≤N−14NlogNN-(N-q)\log q\le N-\tfrac14N\log N, since b≥2b\ge2. There are at most (n+1)2n2(n+1)2^{n^2} subspaces, by counting ordered spanning sets of each dimension. This factor contributes o(N)o(N) to the exponent.

Primitive exceptions and periodic chains

The number of conjugacy classes of primitive subgroups of SNS_N is at most Ncμ(N)N^{c\mu(N)} for an absolute constant cc, where μ(N)\mu(N) is the largest exponent in the prime factorization of NN. Here μ(N)=n\mu(N)=n. Every primitive group KK of degree NN excluding ANA_N has |K|<50NN|K|<50N^{\sqrt N}. Pyber–Shalev · Maróti, Corollary 1.1(ii)

Fix one such representative KK. For a bijection gg satisfying g−1Tg≤Kg^{-1}Tg\le K, the images under conjugation of the nn standard translations have at most |K|n|K|^n choices. For each choice, two conjugators differ by a member of the centralizer of TT. A map commuting with every translation is determined by its image of zero, so this centralizer has size NN. Each distinct conjugate gKg−1gKg^{-1} containing TT arises from at least |K||K| conjugators. Multiplying the resulting number of conjugates by |K||K| bounds the number of possible PP for this class by N|K|nN|K|^n.

Summing over classes and dividing by N!N! gives

Pr(G primitive,AN≰G)≤NcnN(50NN)nN!=exp(−NlogN+O(N)). \Pr(G\text{ primitive},\ A_N\nleq G) \le \frac{N^{cn}\,N\,(50N^{\sqrt N})^n}{N!} =\exp(-N\log N+O(N)).

An imprimitive GG gives a disconnected difference graph. A connected periodic chain therefore belongs to the primitive exceptional event just bounded. Combining these estimates with the two-half calculation proves the main equivalent and the conditional statement. Stirling's formula supplies the constant 2π\sqrt{2\pi}.

At t=N−1t=N-1 and t=Nt=N there is a separate exact boundary. For n≥2n\ge2 every translation is even, so every round has sign sgn(P)\mathrm{sgn}(P). At time rr the parity of the full permutation is fixed. Its action on an ordered (N−1)(N-1)-tuple determines the last image as well, leaving half of the targets unreachable at each time. Thus fN−1(n)=fN(n)=1f_{N-1}(n)=f_N(n)=1.

A fixed-order expansion

For sharper estimates let [nd]2[n\;d]_2 denote the binary Gaussian binomial coefficient, the number of subspaces of codimension dd. Define integers

cd=(2d)!−∑j=1d−1[dj]2cj((2d−j)!)2j(d≥1). c_d=(2^d)!-\sum_{j=1}^{d-1} [d\;j]_2 c_j\,((2^{d-j})!)^{2^j}\qquad(d\ge1).

For every fixed k≥1k\ge1, uniformly in 2≤t≤N−22\le t\le N-2,

|ft(n)−1N!∑d=1k[nd]2cd((N/2d)!)2d|≤exp(−(k+1)Nlog2+ok(N)). \left|f_t(n)-\frac{1}{N!}\sum_{d=1}^k [n\;d]_2 c_d\,((N/2^d)!)^{2^d}\right| \le \exp\bigl(-(k+1)N\log2+o_k(N)\bigr).

In particular c1=2c_1=2, c2=0c_2=0, and c3=32,256c_3=32{,}256. The contributions on the four-coset scale cancel. The first nonzero correction to the leading expression is [n3]232,256((N/8)!)8/N![n\;3]_2\,32{,}256\,((N/8)!)^8/N!.

Proof of the coefficients. Use inclusion–exclusion for the union of events that PP preserves cosets of a proper nonzero space WW. Index a nonempty family of distinct WW by its intersection II. Preserving each partition preserves their common refinement, the cosets of II. For fixed I≠0I\ne0 of codimension dd, families with this intersection correspond to families of proper subspaces of V/IV/I having zero intersection, including the possibility of the zero subspace. If ss quotient permutations preserve all members of one family, its full intersection event has s((N/2d)!)2ds\,((N/2^d)!)^{2^d} labeled permutations, by arbitrary bijections inside the fibers. Thus the signed contribution for this II is a universal coefficient cdc_d times this fiber factor.

To evaluate cdc_d, apply the same inclusion–exclusion in dimension dd to all proper subspaces including zero. The union contains every permutation because any permutation preserves the singleton partition. Group by intersection again. The term with zero intersection is cdc_d, so subtracting the terms of codimension j<dj<d from (2d)!(2^d)! gives the displayed recurrence.

Proof of the error. Truncate the signed indicator to families whose intersection has codimension at most kk. Its expectation is precisely the displayed sum. For each table its absolute value is at most the number of retained families. For each possible intersection II, a retained family is a subset of the subspaces of its quotient of dimension at most kk. Thus the number of retained families is at most (n+1)2n2(n+1)2^{n^2} times a constant depending only on kk. Its logarithm is ok(N)o_k(N).

The truncated and true indicators agree unless the intersection of all preserved proper nonzero subspaces has codimension greater than kk. For n>2kn>2k, this exceptional event implies the existence of a preserved nonzero subspace of codimension at least k+1k+1. Indeed, if one of the original subspaces has such codimension we are done. Otherwise take successive intersections until their codimension first exceeds kk. At that step it is at most 2k<n2k<n, and intersections of preserved partitions still give preserved coset partitions. The previous high-codimension bound now controls the expected truncation error, including multiplication by the number of retained families. The primitive exception is smaller at every fixed order. This proves the claimed expansion.

Five bits with finite bounds

Let BnB_n count permutations preserving at least one parity split. The invariant masks form a binary vector space. Fixing a dd-space of masks lets PP translate the 2d2^d fibers of their joint map and permute within them. Inverting on the subspace lattice gives the exact integer

Bn=∑d=1n(−1)d+12d(d−1)/2[nd]22d((N/2d)!)2d. B_n=\sum_{d=1}^n (-1)^{d+1}2^{d(d-1)/2}[n\;d]_2\, 2^d\,((N/2^d)!)^{2^d}.

Equivalently, this follows by downward subtraction of the numbers of larger spaces containing a given mask space. At n=5n=5 the dimension-specific criterion says that each failure is affine or preserves some nontrivial coset partition. An affine map with reducible linear part already preserves one. Irreducible linear parts have order 31 since 3131 is prime. There are six Frobenius orbits on the 30 nonidentity elements of 𝔽32*\mathbb F_{32}^*. Each gives a conjugacy class of |GL(5,2)|/31|\mathrm{GL}(5,2)|/31 matrices, since its centralizer is the group of nonzero field multiplications. Allowing the 32 translations yields exactly J=61,931,520J=61{,}931{,}520 connected periodic permutations. Their irreducibility makes them disjoint from the parity family. Five-bit criterion and the degree-32 classification

Consequently 32!f2(5)32! f_2(5) lies between B5+JB_5+J and

B5+J+∑d=24[5d]2(2d)!((32/2d)!)2d. B_5+J+\sum_{d=2}^4[5\;d]_2\,(2^d)!\,((32/2^d)!)^{2^d}.

The upper bound allows overlaps. The separate congruence-lattice recurrence resolves the exact count. This interval alone places the fraction of failures explained by preserved parity above 99.99996%. With uniform independent samples of five-bit tables, a sample of 10,000 has probability below 0.001032 of encountering even one nonmixer, by a union bound.
